column2: In an unbroken chain of events, which feature identifies the proximate cause of an insured loss?
column3: Its effect in bringing about the damage
column4: Its closeness in time to the claim
column5: Its position at the start of the chain
column7: The court looks for the effective cause in the ordinary course of events. The event nearest in time may simply be a consequence of an earlier peril.

column2: Lightning ignites hay. Crews soak nearby grain while extinguishing the blaze. What proximately caused the grain damage?
column7: Ordinary firefighting does not break the causal chain. Water used to contain the fire damages the grain as a consequence of that insured peril.

column2: Two concurrent causes produce one loss. One is insured and the other is unmentioned. What is the usual outcome?
column5: Cover conditional on both being listed
column7: An insured proximate cause can support the claim when the concurrent cause is outside the insuring clause but is not expressly excluded. The policy wording still governs.

column2: An insured peril and an expressly excluded peril jointly cause indivisible damage. Which provision generally prevails?
column5: Excess applied to the insured peril
column7: Where both perils are proximate causes, an express exclusion generally defeats cover for the indivisible loss. Its effect depends on the wording.

column2: Which amount measures a simple indemnity claim for destroyed stock, assuming full cover at cost?
column7: Indemnity measures the financial loss on the basis the contract specifies. A sum insured is a ceiling, not an automatic payment.

column2: A fixed-benefit policy pays £120 per qualifying hospital night. What is due for four nights if expenses total £350?
column7: The benefit follows the agreed daily rate. Four nights at £120 produce £480 regardless of the actual bills.

column2: A painting insured at an agreed £36,000 is destroyed when its market value is £30,000. What valuation normally applies?
column7: A valid agreed valuation fixes the basis for a covered total loss. The policyholder still has to establish that the loss occurred.

column2: A warehouse insures £600,000 of stock on a £90,000 first-loss basis. What does £90,000 represent?
column7: First-loss cover sets a sum below the total value where losing the whole stock in one event is considered unlikely. The stated amount limits the insurer's payment.

column2: A laptop is stolen under new-for-old cover. Which figure best measures its replacement, before any excess?
column6: Cost of the latest premium model
column7: New-for-old cover looks to a new counterpart of equivalent specification. The original price and the depreciated value answer different questions.

column2: Under a strict pro rata average clause, £300,000 covers a £400,000 building. What is payable on £48,000 damage before excess?
column7: The insured fraction is 300,000 divided by 400,000, or three quarters. Applying that fraction to £48,000 gives £36,000.

column2: Which figure should be compared with the sum insured under a buildings policy written on a reinstatement basis?
column7: The relevant basis is the cost to rebuild the insured structure. A sale price also reflects land and local demand.

column2: An insurer supplies an equivalent watch after a theft. Which settlement method has it chosen?
column7: Supplying another equivalent item replaces the insured article. A cash settlement would leave the purchase to the policyholder.

column2: A provider appoints a contractor to restore a flooded kitchen. Who normally answers for the quality of that work?
column7: The Financial Ombudsman Service ordinarily expects an insurer to put right poor work by a repairer it selected. The position can differ where the customer independently insists on a contractor.

column2: After a fire the insurer commissions builders to reconstruct the destroyed workshop. Which settlement option is this?
column7: Rebuilding the destroyed premises restores the insured property. Paying the policyholder to arrange the work would be a cash settlement.

column2: An insurer transfers the agreed repair cost to the owner, who chooses a contractor. How was the claim settled?
column7: The insurer discharges its obligation by paying money. In a managed repair it would arrange for the work itself.

column2: A claim attracts 80% under a valid average clause. Which share of the assessed damage remains uninsured before excess?
column7: Paying 80% leaves the policyholder to bear the remaining 20%, or one fifth. This follows from the ratio of the sum insured to the value at risk.

column2: Two property insurers cover the same interest against the same fire. One pays the entire loss. What can it seek from the other?
column7: Where the policies share liability, an insurer paying more than its share may seek a contribution from its fellow insurer. Subrogation concerns rights against a party responsible for the damage.

column2: Policies share a £24,000 loss by sums insured of £100,000 and £300,000. What is the smaller policy's share?
column7: The smaller sum is one quarter of the combined £400,000. One quarter of the loss is £6,000.

column2: Two independent liabilities are £6,000 and £9,000 for a £10,000 loss. What share falls to the second insurer on that basis?
column7: Independent liability uses the amount each insurer would owe alone. The second share is 9,000 divided by 15,000 times £10,000.

column2: Which pair of policies could contribute to the same warehouse owner's fire loss?
column3: Two buildings covers on the owner's interest
column5: Fire insurance and employees' accident benefits
column7: Contribution requires overlapping liability for the same interest and loss. Separate owners of a building and its contents generally suffer different losses.

column2: A negligent carrier damages insured machinery. Which right can the insurer exercise after indemnifying the owner?
column7: Subrogation lets an indemnifying insurer exercise the insured's existing rights against the wrongdoer. Payment does not create a stronger cause of action than the insured had.

column2: A policy waives subrogation against a named contractor. How does this affect a covered loss caused by that contractor?
column3: Bars the insurer's recovery from the contractor
column4: Makes the contractor a second insurer
column5: Transfers the policy excess to the contractor
column6: Removes the insured's cover for the damage
column7: A waiver prevents the insurer relying on the specified recovery right. It does not by itself turn damage caused by that contractor into an excluded loss.

column2: A marine insurer pays for partial damage to a consignment. Who retains title to the remaining goods?
column7: Under the Marine Insurance Act a partial-loss payment does not pass ownership of the remaining goods. The insurer can still use the insured's rights to the extent of the indemnity.

column2: How should a marine policyholder treat receipts exceeding the permitted indemnity under overlapping cargo policies?
column3: Hold the surplus for the insurers
column4: Apply it to the next voyage premium
column5: Retain it as a second policy benefit
column6: Credit it to the carrier for freight
column7: The Marine Insurance Act treats the excess as held for the insurers according to their contribution rights. Multiple policies do not increase the permitted indemnity.

column2: A driver in England damages a parked van and her own car. Which repair falls within compulsory third-party cover?
column7: Compulsory cover addresses the driver's liability for damage to other people's property. Damage to her own car needs wider cover.

column2: A London keeper cancels cover on a car stored in a private garage. Which declaration avoids continuous insurance enforcement?
column7: A keeper taking a vehicle off the road in Great Britain can make a SORN. Private storage alone does not end the continuous insurance requirement.

column2: Which claim is the intended subject of employers' liability insurance in Great Britain?
column7: Employers' liability covers legal liability to employees for injury or illness arising from their work. A visitor's claim usually falls under public liability.

column2: Which English company qualifies for the single employee-owner exemption from compulsory employers' liability insurance?
column7: The exemption requires a company to employ only its owner and for that person to hold at least half the issued shares. Collective ownership by several employees is insufficient.

column2: An employer displays its liability certificate electronically. What determines whether this meets the display requirement?
column5: It carries a qualified electronic seal
column7: An electronic certificate is acceptable if employees can reasonably access it and understand how to do so. Public access is not the test.

column2: Who enforces compulsory employers' liability insurance requirements for ordinary employers in Great Britain?
column7: HSE inspectors can require an employer to produce its certificate and check it has adequate compulsory cover.

column2: Under the Consumer Rights Act, which effect identifies an unfair insurance term when it conflicts with good faith?
column3: Significant imbalance to the buyer's detriment
column4: Increase in the premium at renewal
column5: Higher excess than a rival insurer's
column6: Difference from a market standard wording
column7: The statutory test concerns the imbalance in rights and obligations and the detriment it causes the consumer. A term is not unfair merely because it differs from a competitor's.

column2: An unfair policy term can be removed without making the remaining cover unworkable. What happens to the rest?
column4: It lapses at the next renewal
column7: The Consumer Rights Act keeps the rest of the contract in effect where practicable. One unfair term therefore need not end the policy.

column2: A household policy term has two reasonable meanings in the customer's claim. Which interpretation prevails?
column3: Meaning most favourable to the consumer
column5: Meaning that produces the lower premium
column6: Meaning used by the claims adjuster
column7: Section 69 of the Consumer Rights Act resolves such ambiguity in the consumer's favour. This question concerns an individual claim.

column2: Which features can place a core premium term outside a Consumer Rights Act assessment of price adequacy?
column7: The core price exemption requires a transparent term brought sufficiently to the consumer's attention. Including a premium in small print does not by itself satisfy both conditions.

column2: An English policy expressly gives all current apprentices an enforceable benefit. How does the 1999 Act identify them?
column7: A contract can identify a beneficiary by class as well as by name or description. Each apprentice does not have to sign the contract.

column2: An English policy expressly benefits the insured's future children. When must a child exist under the 1999 Act?
column3: By the time they exercise their right
column5: When the insurer signs the proposal
column7: A beneficiary need not exist when the contract is made. The legislation allows enforceable benefits for a person later meeting the stipulated description.

column2: An English policy gives a third party an enforceable benefit subject to arbitration. How must it pursue that benefit?
column4: By a fresh contract with the insurer
column6: By first paying part of the premium
column7: A right under the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act is subject to the terms attached to it. The beneficiary takes the benefit along with its arbitration condition.

column2: An FCA-authorised broker wants to underwrite policies on its own account. What regulatory step does this require?
column5: Notification of a change of trading name
column6: Appointment of a new claims administrator
column7: The broker would move from arranging cover to carrying the risk. An already authorised intermediary must apply to the PRA and FCA to add the insurer activities.

column2: Who supervises the financial soundness of a UK-authorised general insurance company?
column7: The PRA oversees insurers' financial soundness, capital and risk controls. The FCA also supervises insurers, with a conduct remit.

column2: Which group benefits from the PRA's specific insurance objective alongside its general safety and soundness objective?
column7: The PRA's insurance supervision contributes to protection for policyholders. Maintaining shareholder returns is not a statutory prudential objective.

column2: A retail insurer compares total customer charges with cover, exclusions and service. Which Consumer Duty outcome is being tested?
column7: The fair value assessment compares the amount paid with the package of benefits and limitations. The cheapest price need not represent the best value.

column2: An insurer asks customers to explain a flood exclusion after reading its leaflet. What is it testing?
column7: Testing whether people can interpret a limitation gauges the effectiveness of the communication. Counting how many leaflets were sent would measure distribution only.

column2: Customers can buy travel insurance online but face repeated failed calls to cancel. Which Duty outcome is most directly at issue?
column7: Obstacles to cancelling concern the service available after purchase. The example concerns access to that service rather than whether the policy meets a particular travel need.

column2: Which FCA action prevents an individual from performing specified regulated functions?
column7: A prohibition targets an individual's ability to carry out regulated work. A financial penalty instead imposes a monetary sanction.

column2: Which FCA sanction publishes a formal criticism of misconduct without itself imposing a fine?
column7: Public censure records the regulator's criticism. Other powers may separately restrict activities, impose a financial penalty or address customer losses.

column2: An insurer receives an FCA warning notice proposing disciplinary action. What opportunity arises before a decision?
column7: A warning notice sets out proposed action and allows the subject to respond. It does not itself bring the disciplinary process to a final decision.

column2: Which FCA sourcebook sets conduct requirements for selling ordinary household insurance?
column7: ICOBS covers conduct in general insurance business, including identifying the customer's insurance demands and needs. MCOB concerns mortgages.

column2: A broker sells home cover without a personal recommendation. Which check still applies before the sale?
column3: Match between cover and customer needs
column5: Eligibility for a bank's packaged benefits
column6: Assessment of a proposed fund switch
column7: Proposed insurance must meet the customer's demands and needs whether or not advice is given. A non-advised sale still requires this check.

column2: A broker recommends a particular household policy. What must accompany its demands and needs statement?
column7: An advised household sale requires a personalised explanation of the fit. A general product description does not explain why the contract suits that customer.

column2: What should determine development hours for staff distributing general insurance under the revised FCA rules?
column7: Firms must maintain competence and tailor continuing development to staff duties. The FCA removed the compulsory fixed annual hours requirement for these staff.

column2: A broker holds premium payments as the insurer's agent under a risk transfer agreement. Who bears the intermediary credit risk on those premiums?
column7: The written agreement authorises the broker to accept the money for the insurer. The insurer consequently bears the risk of its agent holding the premiums.

column2: A broker collects premiums for an insurer as its agent. What establishes this risk transfer arrangement?
column7: The insurer must agree in writing to the agency arrangement and its scope. A consumer payment instruction alone does not transfer that risk.

column2: A UK insurer breaches its minimum capital requirement. Within what period should it regain compliance under an approved finance scheme?
column7: The PRA's minimum capital breach timetable allows three months from observation of the breach for compliance with the approved finance scheme. The period runs from observation, not from the regulator's later approval of the plan.

column2: An insurer in difficulty provides income protection. Which payment is the PRA particularly concerned to preserve?
column7: The PRA seeks continuity of payments policyholders rely on for essentials. Owners and providers of capital have a different interest in the firm's remaining assets.

column2: Which document proposes how an insurer will restore compliance after breaching its minimum capital requirement?
column7: The PRA assesses the insurer's finance scheme for restoring the minimum capital position. A product value review addresses conduct, not the firm's capital deficit.

column2: Which filing supports ongoing supervision after a UK general insurer receives authorisation?
column7: Authorised insurers continue to report on finances, risk and conduct. Authorisation starts ongoing supervision and does not remove the reporting obligations.
